title: Lightning Incident Response: Triage Patterns, Runbooks, and Customer Templates
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview
--------
This document defines a lightweight, repeatable response pattern for "lightning" incidents — service degradations that are detected and resolved within a short window (target containment < 10 minutes). The goal is to reduce cognitive load on responders, accelerate safe remediation, and provide consistent, quick customer-facing communications when impact is brief but visible.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: Redwood public inference-hosting and gateway services (API, routing, model-fanout).
- Excludes: long-running incidents (active > 60 minutes), security incidents (see security-and-compliance policies), and on-prem private deployments (follow private deployment runbooks).

When to use this pattern
------------------------
Use the lightning pattern when all of the following are true:
1) Alert type matches a lightning signature (see detection rules below).
2) Estimated customer-impact window is low (automated fallback available or small fraction of traffic).
3) Primary remediation is reversible or a safe fallback exists (model downgrade, region-fallback, circuit-breaker).

Key outcomes
------------
- Contain impact and restore service within 10 minutes.
- Provide a short customer status message when impact is user-visible.
- Capture minimal post-incident notes and a tag for later retrospective if incidents repeat.

Lightning detection signatures (examples)
----------------------------------------
Use monitoring rules that map to the following signatures. These are examples; teams should tune thresholds per service.

- API 5xx spike: 5xx rate > 3% for 1 minute AND 5xx traffic spike > 15/min compared to rolling baseline.
- P99 latency blip: P99 latency > 3x baseline for 1 minute AND total error rate < 0.5% (indicates degradation, not full outage).
- Model fallback loop: > 20 automatic model-fallback events in 5m window.
- Prefix cache miss storm: cache miss rate increase > 40% leading to sudden CPU/GPU scheduling backlog.

Automated detection rule (Prometheus-like example)
--------------------------------------------------
alert: LightningApi5xx
expr: increase(redwood_api_responses_total{status=~"5.."}[1m]) / increase(redwood_api_requests_total[1m]) > 0.03
for: 0m
labels:
  severity: high
annotations:
  summary: "Lightning 5xx spike on {{ $labels.service }}"

Triage decision graph (high-level)
----------------------------------
1) Alert fires -> primary on-call notified.
2) On-call executes lightning checklist (fast path): confirm alert validity, check automated mitigations, enable fallback if required.
3) If contained within 10 minutes -> close alert, publish brief status note, and create an incident-lite entry.
4) If not contained -> escalate to standard incident process and promote to full incident bridge.

Lightning checklist (fast path) — run by primary on-call
------------------------------------------------------
1. Confirm: Validate alert (metrics, traces, recent deploys).
2. Mitigate: If automation exists, confirm it ran; otherwise run the recommended mitigation.
3. Stabilize: Reduce blast radius (route to warm region, enable canary model, scale up routing instances).
4. Communicate: Post short customer status (template below).
5. Tag: Create an incident-lite ticket with minimal fields (impact, remediation, owner, timeline).
6. Observe: Monitor for 15 minutes post-remediation before closing.

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Primary on-call (engineer): validate and run lightning checklist.
- Secondary on-call: available for immediate escalation if primary needs help.
- Ops comms owner (rotation-based): approves customer message and publishes to status page if public.
- Incident owner (only if escalated): takes over when > 10 minutes or wider impact.

Sample mitigations matrix
------------------------
| Symptom | Fast mitigation | Safe fallback | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model oom / memory errors | Restart model worker (graceful) | Route traffic to smaller quantized model | Serving runtime on-call |
| P99 spikes due to KV eviction | Evict non-critical keys, increase cache TTL | Enable prefix-KV cache bypass (degraded cost) | Runtime infra |
| Routing controller flaps | Restart controller pod, apply circuit-breaker | Route to alternate region | Gateway team |
| Sudden 5xx spike | Rollback last deploy (if correlates) | Switch to stable model version | Deploy owner |

Runbook snippets (examples)
---------------------------
Runbook: Fast model worker restart
1. Identify affected model worker set: kubectl get pods -l app=model-worker -n serving | grep -i <model-name>
2. Drain connections: curl -X POST http://<worker-ip>:3000/drain || true
3. Restart: kubectl rollout restart statefulset/model-worker-<model-name> -n serving
4. Validate: watch -n1 kubectl logs -l app=model-worker -n serving --tail 50 | grep "started"

CLI automation example (safe rollback)
------------------------------------
# safe-rollback.sh
#!/bin/bash
SERVICE=$1
kubectl -n serving rollout undo deployment/$SERVICE --to-revision=stable || echo "rollback failed"

Customer-facing status templates (short, public)
------------------------------------------------
Use these when a user-visible degradation is detected but service is largely available. Keep messages concise and time-bounded.

- Initial (10 min window):
"We detected a brief degradation affecting inference requests to the API. Our on-call team has implemented an automatic mitigation and we expect full service to be restored within 10 minutes. We will post an update when the issue is resolved. Reference: incident #<id>."

- Update (after mitigation, within 30 minutes):
"Service restored. We observed a short degradation affecting a subset of API requests. Mitigation: automatic model fallback. No customer data was exposed. A short incident note has been filed."

Incident-lite ticket schema (minimum fields)
------------------------------------------
| field | example |
|---|---|
| title | "Light: 5xx spike on inference-api (region-us-west)" |
| impact | "Brief increase in 5xx for ~7 minutes; <0.5% customer error rate" |
| start_time | "2026-02-27T14:02:00Z" |
| mitigations | "Enabled fallback model; restarted routing pod" |
| owner | "Aisha Patel" |
| postmortem_required | "auto: no, review_if_repeat: yes" |

Post-incident actions (lightweight)
-----------------------------------
- If incident-lite recurs 3x in 30 days, schedule a retro and convert to a full postmortem.
- Maintain a rolling log of lightning incidents per service for trending (Ops: lightning-incidents-YYYYMM.csv).
- Add any automation gaps found during the incident to the backlog with severity P2 or higher.

Game-day scenarios and exercises
-------------------------------
Recommended quarterly game-day focused on lightning patterns. Example scenarios:
1. Rapid 5xx spike originating from a single model version. Objective: validate automatic model-fallback and rollback script.
2. Prefix cache miss storm. Objective: confirm cache TTL adjustments and observe scheduling backlog behavior.
3. Region routing flaps under load. Objective: validate cross-region routing and customer status pipeline.

Success criteria for a game-day drill
- Containment within 10 minutes for >= 75% of runs.
- Clear owner assigned within 90 seconds.
- Customer message posted within 5 minutes when impact is visible.

Governance and metrics
----------------------
Track the following metrics to ensure the lightning pattern is effective:
- Mean time to contain (MTTC) for lightning incidents. Target: <= 6 minutes.
- Percent of lightning incidents auto-contained (no escalation). Target: >= 80%.
- Repeat rate: % of services with >=3 lightning incidents in 30 days. Target: <= 5%.

Appendices
---------
A. Quick decision ladder (one-line rules)
- If 5xx spike AND automatic mitigation exists -> run mitigation, observe 15m, close if stable.
- If mitigation fails twice OR impact grows -> escalate immediately to oncall ladder.

B. Template automation alert rule (example JSON for alert manager)
{
  "alert": "LightningLatency",
  "expr": "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_api_request_latency_bucket[1m])) by (le)) > 0.03",
  "for": "0m",
  "labels": {"severity":"high","category":"lightning"},
  "annotations": {"summary":"P99 spike on {{ $labels.service }}"}
}

C. Lightweight post-incident checklist for documentation
- Timestamped timeline (start, mitigation start, recovery).
- Short description of root cause if known.
- Automation gap and follow-up owner.
- Action items assigned with due dates.

D. Links and references
